key_terms.meaning: Processing that amplifies, filters, linearises and isolates a sensor output before digitisation.
Device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, e.g. a thermocouple gives volts per °C.
Switch that connects one of many sensor channels to a single ADC input in a chosen order.
Circuit that freezes the analogue input while the ADC converts it, so the value does not change mid-conversion.
ADC that tests bits from MSB to LSB, taking n clock steps for an n-bit result.
Oversampling ADC that trades high sample rate for high resolution using noise shaping and digital filtering.
Transmission standard where 4 mA marks zero and 20 mA full scale; current stays the same along a series loop.
Unwanted path formed when two grounded points sit at different potentials, causing current and noise in a signal cable.
Actuator that converts compressed air pressure into force using a cylinder or diaphragm.
Actuator that converts pressurised oil into large force using a cylinder, motor or rotary vane.
Coil that pulls a magnetic plunger through a short stroke when current flows.
Electrically operated switch whose coil moves contacts to open or close a separate circuit.
Motor that rotates in fixed steps when pulses arrive; step angle θ = 360°/N for N steps per revolution.
Motor with position or speed feedback that corrects error until output follows the command.
Actuator that strains when voltage is applied; strain is small but fast and forceful, with little heat.
Metal that changes shape on heating above a transition temperature and can return on cooling.
Four-arm resistive bridge balanced when R1/R3 = R2/Rx (arms A–B, B–D, A–C, C–D), giving zero detector voltage.
AC bridge that measures unknown inductance by balancing it against a known capacitance and resistance.
Amplifier that passes signal while blocking direct electrical connection, breaking ground loops and protecting circuits.
Oscilloscope that samples, digitises and stores a waveform so one-time events can be displayed.
AC bridge for high-Q coils (Q > 10): series R₁C₁ arm, Lx = R₂R₃C₁/(1 + ω²R₁²C₁²), Q = 1/(ωR₁C₁).
High-voltage AC bridge for capacitance and loss: Cx = C₂R₄/R₃, tan δ = ωR₄C₄.
Common-mode rejection ratio, 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub>) in dB; an ECG amplifier needs about 100 dB.
Spot movement per plate volt in a CRT, S = L l /(2 d V<sub>a</sub>), in m/V.

takeaways: Signal conditioning must match the sensor output range and impedance to the ADC input range and must reject noise before conversion.
A data acquisition system is only as good as its weakest link: resolution, sampling rate, settling time and channel order all matter.
Current loops and differential transmission protect small signals over long distances.
Pneumatic actuators suit clean, spark-free, moderate-force work; hydraulic actuators suit high force.
Solenoids and relays give on/off motion; motors give continuous motion.
Stepper motors are simple open-loop positioners; servo motors use feedback for accuracy under load.
Micro actuators are chosen for small size and speed, not for large force.
Bridges measure unknown R, L or C by null balance, and display instruments trade bandwidth against accuracy.

In medicine the same chain is the ECG front end (instrumentation amplifier, 0.05 Hz high-pass, notch, isolation), the patient monitor that samples and displays it, and the pumps and valves that act on the patient.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to carry block diagrams, bridge balance conditions, ADC and actuator comparisons, and clear calculations with units, not just definitions. Biomedical syllabi stress the bridges (Wheatstone, Kelvin, Maxwell, Hay, Schering), the filters (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, notch), pre-amplifiers, differential and isolation amplifiers, and the display devices (DVM, multimeter, CRO with CRT deflection, DSO and spectrum analyser).

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a data acquisition system and explain the job of each block.
outline: Transducer and signal conditioner
Multiplexer and sample-and-hold
ADC and processor or controller
Store, display or bus interface

answer.text: Block diagram. The blocks sit in signal order:
answer.pre:
transducers → signal conditioners → multiplexer → sample-and-hold → ADC → processor / controller → store, display or bus
                                   ↑ channel select and convert commands from the processor

answer: Transducer. Converts the physical variable (temperature, pressure, strain, a heartbeat) into an electrical quantity: millivolts from a thermocouple or bridge, a resistance change from an RTD, a current from a photodiode.

Signal conditioner. Amplifies, filters, linearises and isolates each sensor output to a standard range such as 0 to 5 V or ±5 V. Its low-pass filter (the anti-aliasing filter) removes components above half the channel's sample rate before sampling, because nothing after the multiplexer can remove them.

Multiplexer. An analogue switch bank that connects one channel at a time to the shared converter, in the order the processor chooses. It lets one accurate ADC serve 8, 16 or more channels; the price is that the converter's speed is shared, fch = ftotal/N.

Sample-and-hold. Closes a switch to charge a capacitor to the input (acquisition), then opens it and holds the value while the ADC converts. It removes the error from the input moving during the conversion; what remains is the aperture error, (rate of change) × (aperture time).
ADC. Converts the held voltage into an n-bit number. The bit count fixes the resolution, ΔV = VFS/2ⁿ, and the converter type (SAR, flash, sigma-delta) fixes the speed.
Processor or controller. Selects channels, starts conversions, scales the counts into engineering units (°C, kPa, mmHg), applies calibration and alarm limits, and time-stamps the readings.
Store, display or bus. Keeps the data in memory, shows it on a screen, or sends it over RS-485, USB, Ethernet or a fieldbus to a supervisory computer.

answer.text: Worked numbers. 8 channels, ±5 V input, 12-bit ADC, 4 channels scanned at 1 kS/s each:

answer: Medical example. A bedside monitor is a DAS: three ECG leads at 500 S/s, a pulse-oximeter waveform at 100 S/s and an arterial pressure at 250 S/s share one 16-bit converter running at 1850 S/s, with 540.5 µs per conversion.

Check. The 250 µs per conversion must hold multiplexer settling, sample-and-hold acquisition and the ADC's own conversion; a SAR converter of 10 µs leaves ample margin, and 500 Hz per channel is more than a 0.05 to 150 Hz ECG needs.

bank.q: Define signal conditioning. List and explain amplification, filtering, linearisation and isolation.
outline: Definition and need near the sensor
Amplification for small signals
Filtering to remove noise and aliasing
Linearisation and electrical isolation
answer: Definition. Signal conditioning is the processing between a sensor and the next stage (ADC, transmitter, display) that turns a weak, noisy, non-linear, possibly unsafe sensor output into a clean signal of standard range, for example 0 to 5 V or 4 to 20 mA. It is done close to the sensor so noise and cable losses act on a large, robust signal.

answer.text: Amplification. Raises a millivolt signal to the ADC range. An instrumentation amplifier is used because it has a very high input impedance (it does not load a bridge) and a high CMRR (it rejects the volts of common-mode offset on both bridge outputs). Gain and its decibel value:
answer.pre:
G = R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub> = 100 kΩ / 200 Ω = 500;  G<sub>dB</sub> = 20 log₁₀ 500 = 54.0 dB
2 mV × 500 = 1.0 V

answer: Gain multiplies the offset and noise too: 0.1 mV of input offset becomes 50 mV. Large signals need the opposite, attenuation by a divider, and the next stage must have an input resistance well above the source resistance (impedance matching in the measurement sense).

answer.text: Filtering. Removes interference outside the signal band: 50 Hz mains hum, switching-supply noise, radio pickup, and anything above half the sample rate that would alias. A first-order RC low-pass:

answer: A filter also delays the signal and slows a step (time constant RC), so f<sub>c</sub> is placed above the highest real signal frequency and below the noise.

Linearisation. Makes the output proportional to the measured quantity when the sensor is not linear (thermocouple polynomial, thermistor exponential). Hardware breakpoint circuits add slope corrections between reference levels; software uses a calibration table and interpolates. Worked value: table points 2010 counts at 36.0 °C and 1890 counts at 38.0 °C give, for 1950 counts, T = 36.0 + (1950 − 2010)(2.0)/(1890 − 2010) = 37.0 °C.

Isolation. Breaks the direct conducting path between the sensor side and the computer side, by a transformer, an optocoupler or a capacitive barrier in an isolation amplifier. It breaks ground loops (two earths at different potentials driving current through the signal cable), protects the electronics from surges on long cables, and protects people: an ECG front end floats the patient side so that leakage current stays at microamperes.
Other jobs. Excitation (a bridge or RTD needs a stable supply), cold-junction compensation for thermocouples, surge clamping, and conversion between voltage and current for transmission.

Check. With the numbers above, the 2 mV bridge signal leaves the amplifier at 1.0 V while 1 V of 50 Hz hum at the filter input would leave it at 0.303 V; a second filter order or a notch is needed if the hum must be below 1 % of the signal.

bank.q: Compare a stepper motor and a servo motor on motion, feedback, cost and load behaviour.
outline: Stepper moves in fixed steps, often open-loop
Servo uses encoder or resolver feedback
Servo corrects error under load
Cost and complexity comparison
answer: Stepper motor. A motor whose rotor moves one fixed angle for each input pulse. Step angle θs = 360°/N; a hybrid stepper has 1.8°, N = 200. Position is the count of pulses sent, so no sensor is needed.

Servo motor. A DC or AC (synchronous) motor inside a closed loop: an encoder, resolver or potentiometer measures the shaft, the drive computes the error e = r − y and drives current to reduce it. It can run in position, speed or torque mode.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Aspect
Stepper
Servo
rows: discrete steps; smooth only with microstepping
falls quickly as pulse rate rises
nearly constant up to rated speed
error grows and is corrected; drive can alarm
holds with full torque, draws current
holds by feedback; may dither slightly
higher; loop gains must be tuned

answer: Motion in numbers. A 1.8° stepper at 1000 pulses/s turns at 1000/200 = 5 rev/s = 300 rpm; on a 5 mm lead screw it moves 25 mm/s and 0.025 mm per step. A servo with a 2500-count encoder on a 10 mm lead resolves 10/2500 = 0.004 mm per count and needs 12 500 counts for 50 mm.

Load behaviour. If the load torque exceeds the stepper's pull-in torque at the commanded rate, or the pulse rate is ramped too fast, the rotor slips and every later position is wrong, with no indication. The servo measures the actual angle, so a sudden load produces an error that the drive corrects with more current; if it cannot, it reports a following-error fault.

Resonance and smoothness. Steppers can resonate near their natural frequency and lose steps; half-stepping, microstepping or damping help. Servos have no such step resonance but can oscillate if the loop gain is too high.
Cost and complexity. A stepper and driver are cheap and need no tuning; a servo needs an encoder, a more complex drive and commissioning. Closed-loop steppers with encoders sit between the two.

Medical example. A syringe pump uses a stepper: the load is light and steady, and 1/16 microstepping on a 1 mm lead gives 0.175 µL per microstep from a 50 mL syringe. A surgical robot uses servos because the load changes and the position must be known exactly.
Check. 300 rpm × 200 steps/rev / 60 s = 1000 steps/s, the pulse rate applied; the servo needs 50 / 0.004 = 12 500 counts, as found.

bank.q: A thermocouple gives 8 mV at 200 °C and 0 mV at 0 °C. Design a signal conditioner to give 0–5 V; find gain and explain the filter and isolation you add.
outline: Gain = 5 V / 8 mV = 625
Use instrumentation or differential amplifier
Add low-pass filter for noise
Add isolation to break ground loops
answer: Requirement. 0 to 200 °C gives 0 to 8 mV (40 µV/°C); the output must be 0 to 5 V for an ADC.
Gain. G = 5 V / 8 mV = 625, about 55.9 dB (20 log₁₀ 625).

answer.text: Amplifier. A three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier, because the thermocouple signal is tiny, floating, and sits on common-mode noise picked up by the leads. With the input stage setting all the gain and a unity-gain difference stage:

answer: A chopper-stabilised or zero-drift amplifier is preferred: a drift of only 1 µV/°C would be 0.025 °C of error per degree of ambient change.

Cold-junction compensation. The thermocouple measures the difference between the hot junction and the terminal block. At 25 °C ambient the terminals subtract 25 × 40 µV = 1.0 mV, so a temperature sensor at the terminals (thermistor, IC sensor) adds back 1.0 mV equivalent, in hardware or in software.

answer.text: Filter. Temperature changes slowly, so a low cutoff is allowed. An RC low-pass of R = 16 kΩ, C = 10 µF:

answer: The filter also sets the anti-aliasing limit for the ADC. A differential RC filter at the amplifier input, or an integrating (sigma-delta) ADC timed to 20 ms multiples, rejects 50 Hz further.
Linearisation. A type K thermocouple is close to linear over 0 to 200 °C, but the processor should use the standard polynomial or a table for better than about 1 °C.

Isolation. The thermocouple may touch an earthed or high-voltage metal part; an isolation amplifier or isolated ADC after the gain stage breaks the ground loop between that earth and the logger's earth, and survives surges. Its working voltage must exceed the highest continuous voltage between the two grounds.

answer.text: Resolution check. With a 12-bit ADC on 0 to 5 V:

answer: Check. 100 °C gives 4 mV × 625 = 2.5 V, half of the 5 V range for half of the 200 °C span, so the chain is linear end to end.

bank.q: An 8-bit ADC has reference 5 V. Find resolution and output code for 2.0 V; state one error source.
outline: Resolution = 5/255 ≈ 19.6 mV
Quantisation error of ±½ LSB
Reference drift or missing sample-and-hold
answer: Convention. This book uses ΔV = VFS/2ⁿ; some texts use VFS/(2ⁿ − 1) for the step between the first and last codes. Both are shown so the answer matches either marking scheme.

answer.text: Resolution.
answer.pre:
ΔV = 5 V / 2⁸ = 5 / 256 = 19.53 mV   (book convention)
ΔV = 5 V / 255 = 19.61 mV          (alternative convention)

answer.text: Output code for 2.0 V.

answer: With the 255 convention the ideal code is 2.0/0.01961 = 102.0, also 102, so both give the same answer here.

SAR trace. A successive approximation converter finds this code in 8 clock steps: try 128 (2.5 V, too high, bit 7 = 0); 64 (1.25 V, keep, bit 6 = 1); 96 (1.875 V, keep, bit 5 = 1); 112 (2.1875 V, too high, 0); 104 (2.031 V, too high, 0); 100 (1.953 V, keep, 1); 102 (1.992 V, keep, 1); 103 (2.012 V, too high, 0). Result 0110 0110 = 102.

Quantisation error. The code covers a band one LSB wide, so the reading is uncertain by up to one LSB with truncation (0 to 19.5 mV) or ±½ LSB (±9.77 mV) with rounding. Here 2.0 − 1.992 = 8 mV lies within one LSB.

Other error sources (any one). Reference error or drift: a 1 % low reference (4.95 V) makes every code 1 % high, 2.0/(4.95/256) = 103.4, so the code becomes 103. Offset and gain errors of the converter. Missing sample-and-hold: if the input changes during the 8 steps, early and late bits are decided on different voltages. Noise larger than one LSB makes the last bit flicker.
Improving it. More bits (a 12-bit ADC gives 1.22 mV steps), a precision reference, an input range matched to the signal, and averaging several readings.
Check. 102 × 19.53 mV = 1.992 V and 103 × 19.53 mV = 2.012 V bracket 2.0 V, so 102 is the correct truncated code.

bank.q: A 4–20 mA transmitter reads 12 mA. Find the percentage of full scale and the voltage across a 250 Ω receiver resistor.
outline: Voltage V = I × R = 12 mA × 250 Ω = 3 V
4 mA is live zero, not 0 % current
Loop supply must exceed total voltage drop
answer: The standard. A 4 to 20 mA loop carries 0 % of range as 4 mA (the live zero) and 100 % as 20 mA, so the span is 16 mA. A current of 0 mA means a broken loop or a dead transmitter, not a zero reading.

answer.text: Percentage of full scale.

answer: The common slip is 12/20 = 60 %, which forgets the live zero.

answer.text: Receiver voltage.
The full scale on the receiver.

answer: In engineering units. If the transmitter is ranged 0 to 150 °C, 50 % is 75 °C; if it is ranged 0 to 10 bar, 5 bar. The receiver computes value = low + (V − 1)/(5 − 1) × (high − low).

Loop supply. The supply must cover the transmitter's minimum voltage, the sense resistor and the cable at 20 mA. With a 24 V supply and a transmitter needing 10 V, Rloop,max = (24 − 10)/0.020 = 700 Ω, which includes the 250 Ω resistor, leaving 450 Ω for the cable both ways.

Why the reading is robust. Every element of the series loop carries the same current, so cable resistance changes only the voltage the supply must provide, not the current; and a current is not changed by a few volts of ground difference between the two ends, which would corrupt a voltage signal.
Faults the receiver can flag. Below about 3.8 mA or above about 20.5 mA the reading is outside the normal band, which many systems treat as a sensor or wiring fault.
Check. 3.0 V on the 1 to 5 V scale is (3 − 1)/(5 − 1) = 50 %, the same as from the current.

bank.q: A hydraulic cylinder has piston area 0.005 m² and oil pressure 10 MPa. Find force; choose it over a pneumatic cylinder for a press and justify.
outline: Force F = p × A = 10 MPa × 0.005 m² = 50 kN
Hydraulic oil gives high force in small size
Pneumatic air is compressible and spark-free
Press needs stiffness and force, so hydraulic suits

answer.text: Force.
answer.pre: F = p A = 10 × 10⁶ Pa × 0.005 m² = 5.0 × 10⁴ N = 50 kN  (about 5.1 tonnes-force)

answer: The piston area 0.005 m² is a bore of √(4 × 0.005/π) = 0.0798 m, about 80 mm. With a mechanical efficiency of 0.9 the usable force would be 45 kN.

answer.text: What a pneumatic cylinder would need. At 6 bar (6 × 10⁵ Pa):

answer: The pneumatic cylinder would need about 17 times the area of the hydraulic one (0.0833/0.005), so it would be large, use a great deal of air per stroke, and still be soft.

Why hydraulic suits a press. (1) Force density: 100 to 200 bar oil gives tens of kilonewtons from a compact cylinder. (2) Stiffness: oil is nearly incompressible, so the ram holds position under load and presses evenly; compressed air would spring back. (3) Controlled slow motion: a flow-control or servo valve gives a smooth, slow approach and a controlled pressing force. (4) Overload protection: the relief valve sets the maximum pressure and so the maximum force, protecting the tool. (5) Holding: a check valve can hold the force without running the pump.

What the pneumatic option still offers. Air is clean, cheap, spark-free and fast for light work; it suits pick-and-place, clamps and packaging. It is chosen for a press only when the force is small, for example a few hundred newtons for stamping labels.

answer.text: Comparison for this duty.

answer: Safety. Hydraulic presses need guards, two-hand controls and pressure-rated hoses, because a burst hose at 10 MPa can inject oil through skin.
Check. 10 MPa = 100 bar, the low end of the 100 to 200 bar range; at 200 bar the same cylinder would give 100 kN, so the choice leaves room to grow.

bank.q: A stepper motor has 200 steps/rev and drives a 5 mm pitch lead screw. Find pulses to move 20 mm; state whether feedback is needed.
outline: 20 mm / 5 mm = 4 revolutions
Open-loop works if load never exceeds torque
Feedback needed if steps may be lost

answer.text: Pulses for 20 mm.

head: Step
Working
Result
rows: lead of a single-start 5 mm pitch screw

answer: If the screw were two-start, the lead would be 10 mm and only 400 pulses would be needed: the travel per revolution, not the thread spacing, is what counts.

Time and speed. At 1000 pulses/s the move takes 0.8 s and the shaft turns 1000/200 = 5 rev/s = 300 rpm, moving the table at 25 mm/s. In half-step mode N becomes 400, so 1600 pulses are needed for the same 20 mm.

Is feedback needed? Not if the motor is sized correctly. A stepper moves exactly one step per pulse as long as the load torque stays below the pull-in torque at the commanded rate, the pulse rate is ramped up and down within the motor's capability, and nothing jams the axis. Under those conditions counting pulses gives the position, and the system runs open loop: printers, 3D printers and syringe pumps work this way.

When feedback is needed. When the load varies or may exceed the torque (a cutting force, a collision), when missed steps would be dangerous or costly (a medical pump, a machine tool), or when the axis must be found again after power loss. Then an encoder checks the actual position (a closed-loop stepper), or a servo motor is used. A home switch at one end is the minimum: it gives a reference at start-up.
Margin. A common rule is to size the motor so its torque at the working speed is at least 1.5 to 2 times the load torque, which keeps the open-loop drive safe.
Resolution. 0.025 mm per full step; with 1/16 microstepping, 0.0016 mm per microstep commanded, though the mechanical accuracy is still set by the full step and the screw.
Check. 800 pulses × 0.025 mm = 20 mm, as required.

bank.q: A signal cable runs 80 m beside a motor drive. Choose voltage or current transmission, explain shielding and grounding, and calculate loop voltage at 20 mA through 100 Ω.
outline: Prefer 4–20 mA current loop for long runs
Use twisted pair with shield grounded at one end
Avoid ground loops and use differential input
answer: The threat. A motor drive switches hundreds of volts in nanoseconds, so the 80 m cable picks up electric (capacitive) and magnetic (inductive) interference, and the drive's earth may sit several volts away from the control-room earth.

Choice: a 4 to 20 mA current loop. In a series loop the current is the same everywhere, set by the transmitter; cable resistance and induced voltages change only the voltage across the loop, not the current. A ground difference that would add directly to a voltage signal does not change a current. The live zero (4 mA) also reveals a broken cable as 0 mA.

answer.text: Voltage transmission for comparison. A 0 to 10 V signal with 1 V of ground difference between the ends reads 10 % of span wrong; the same 1 V in series with a current loop needs only 1 V more from the supply.

head: Effect
0–10 V signal
4–20 mA loop
rows: divider error with the input resistance

answer: Shielding. Use twisted pair, which makes both wires pick up the same magnetic interference so it cancels in the receiver. Put an overall foil or braid screen around the pair to stop electric fields coupling to the conductors.

Grounding. Connect the screen to earth at one end only, normally the receiver (control-room) end; earthing both ends would let the ground difference drive current along the screen, a ground loop. Keep the signal cable in a separate tray, at least 0.3 m from the motor cables, and cross them at right angles. Use an isolated input or isolator at the receiver if the loop must float.

answer.text: Loop voltage.
answer.pre: V = I R = 0.020 A × 100 Ω = 2.0 V at full scale (0.4 V at 4 mA)

answer: Supply budget. With a 250 Ω receiver resistor (5 V at 20 mA), the 100 Ω cable (2 V) and a transmitter needing 10 V, the supply must give at least 10 + 5 + 2 = 17 V at 20 mA; a 24 V supply leaves 7 V of margin. The maximum total resistance on 24 V is (24 − 10)/0.020 = 700 Ω.
Filtering at the receiver. A small RC filter (for example 1 kΩ and 1 µF, fc = 159 Hz) after the sense resistor removes the residual switching noise without slowing a process signal.
Check. 250 + 100 = 350 Ω is half of the 700 Ω limit, so the loop can still reach 20 mA with room for a longer run.

bank.q: Compare flash, SAR and sigma-delta ADCs on speed, resolution, cost and noise; select one for audio and one for a slow temperature logger.
outline: Flash: fastest, low resolution, many comparators
SAR: medium speed, good resolution, common choice
Sigma-delta: slow to medium, high resolution, filters noise
Audio suits sigma-delta; temperature logger suits sigma-delta or SAR
answer: Flash ADC. A resistor ladder sets 2ⁿ − 1 reference levels and one comparator sits at each level. All comparators decide at once, and a thermometer-to-binary encoder gives the output in a single clock. An 8-bit flash needs 2⁸ − 1 = 255 comparators; a 10-bit one needs 1023. Speed reaches hundreds of megasamples to gigasamples per second, but the comparator count doubles with every bit, so power, chip area, input capacitance and cost rise steeply and practical resolution stops near 8 bits.

answer.text: Successive approximation (SAR) ADC. One comparator, a DAC and a register perform a binary search, one bit per clock, most significant bit first. Trace for a 4-bit SAR, Vref = 16 V, input 11.3 V:

answer: The result 1011 = 11 is found in n = 4 clocks. Conversion time is n clock periods, so a 16-bit SAR at 16 MHz with a few clocks overhead runs at about 1 MS/s. It needs a sample-and-hold, because the input must not change during the search. Resolution of 12 to 18 bits, moderate power and low cost make it the general-purpose converter of microcontrollers and data loggers.

Sigma-delta ADC. A 1-bit (or few-bit) modulator samples far faster than the Nyquist rate and feeds back its own output through an integrator, so the average of the bit stream follows the input. The loop pushes the quantisation noise up to high frequencies (noise shaping), and a digital decimation filter removes it and reduces the rate. Audio converters sample at 64 × 48 kHz = 3.072 MHz and deliver 24-bit words at 48 kS/s. The digital filter also gives very sharp anti-aliasing, so the analogue filter in front can be a simple RC. The price is latency (the filter delay) and that it is poor for multiplexing many channels.

answer.text: Ideal noise floor. SNR = 6.02 n + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine:
answer.pre:
12 bits: 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74.0 dB
16 bits: 6.02 × 16 + 1.76 = 98.08 dB
24 bits: 6.02 × 24 + 1.76 = 146.2 dB (real parts reach about 120 dB, set by analogue noise)

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Criterion
Flash
SAR
Sigma-delta
rows: medium: 100 kS/s to a few MS/s
slow to medium: up to about 1 MS/s, with latency
set by bits and S/H; needs a good anti-alias filter
lowest in band, by oversampling and noise shaping

answer: Choice for audio. Sigma-delta. Audio needs 20 Hz to 20 kHz with about 100 dB of dynamic range, which a 24-bit sigma-delta at 48 kS/s gives, with its own sharp digital anti-aliasing filter. Flash cannot reach the resolution, and a SAR would need a steep analogue filter at 20 kHz.

Choice for a slow temperature logger. A sampling rate of one reading per second is tiny for any converter, so the choice is set by resolution and mains rejection. A sigma-delta converter is the best fit for a thermocouple or RTD: 24 bits resolve microvolts, and a decimation filter with notches at 50 Hz rejects the hum. A 12- to 16-bit SAR is the cheaper choice when many channels are multiplexed or the sensor already gives volts; flash would waste power and give too few bits.

Check. A type-K thermocouple gives about 41 µV/°C. A 24-bit sigma-delta on ±78 mV has an LSB of 0.156 V / 2²⁴ = 9.3 nV, far below 41 µV, so 0.1 °C is set by noise and the cold junction, not the converter. An 8-bit flash on the same span would give 0.61 mV per step, about 15 °C, useless for the logger.

bank.q: A low-level sensor shows 50 Hz hum and a slowly drifting offset. Analyse likely causes and propose differential amplifier, filtering and isolation.
outline: Hum from mains pickup or ground loop
Drift from temperature, bias current or electrode offset
Differential amplifier rejects common-mode voltage
Low-pass or notch filter and isolation amplifier reduce hum
answer: Causes of 50 Hz hum. (a) Capacitive (electric field) coupling from mains wiring onto high-impedance leads and the body, which appears as a common-mode voltage on both inputs. (b) Inductive coupling, where a 50 Hz magnetic field threads the loop formed by the two signal wires and induces a differential voltage. (c) A ground loop: the sensor and the amplifier are earthed at two points with a few hundred millivolts of 50 Hz between them, and the difference drives current along the signal return. (d) A single-ended input, which cannot tell the hum from the signal.

Causes of slow offset drift. (a) Amplifier offset voltage and bias current changing with temperature. (b) Thermocouple EMFs at junctions of different metals in the wiring and connectors. (c) Sensor effects: a bridge zero that moves with temperature, or an electrode half-cell potential that wanders. (d) Supply and reference drift. Worked value: an amplifier with 2 µV/°C offset drift, in a box that warms by 20 °C, at a gain of 1000, moves its output by 2 µV × 20 × 1000 = 40 mV.

Differential amplifier. Bring both sensor wires to an instrumentation amplifier, which amplifies Vd = V₁ − V₂ and rejects the common-mode voltage both wires share. Its high input impedance prevents a source-impedance imbalance from turning common-mode hum into differential hum.

answer.text: CMRR calculation. Gain 1000, signal 1 mV, common-mode hum 0.5 V:

answer: At 60 dB the hum is half the signal; at 100 dB it is 0.5 % of it. A four-resistor difference amplifier with 1 % resistors at gain 100 reaches only about 68 dB, so a monolithic instrumentation amplifier with trimmed resistors is used.

Filtering. (a) A low-pass just above the signal band, for example 10 Hz for a temperature or strain signal, gives −14 dB at 50 Hz in first order and −28 dB in second order. (b) When the signal band includes 50 Hz, as in an ECG, a notch filter at 50 Hz removes the hum with a narrow stop band. (c) A digital filter after the ADC can average over exactly one mains period (20 ms) to null the hum. Filtering does not remove drift, because drift is slow; a high-pass (for example 0.05 Hz in an ECG) removes it only when the signal has no DC content.

Drift remedies. Use a zero-drift (chopper-stabilised) amplifier of about 0.05 µV/°C, which brings the 40 mV above down to 1 mV. Take the gain early so later stages matter less, keep the input junctions at one temperature, use ratiometric excitation so a supply drift cancels in a bridge, and auto-zero by reading a shorted input every few seconds and subtracting.

Isolation and grounding. If a ground loop remains, an isolation amplifier or an isolated ADC breaks the conducting path, so the ground difference appears across the barrier and not in the signal. Use twisted pair against magnetic pickup and a screen earthed at one end only. In a medical front end, isolation also protects the patient, and a driven right-leg circuit feeds back the inverted common-mode voltage to cut it further.

Check. With 100 dB CMRR the hum is 5 mV against a 1.0 V signal, and a second-order 10 Hz low-pass would cut that to about 0.2 mV; the zero-drift amplifier keeps drift at 1 mV for 20 °C. Both errors are now near 0.1 % of the signal.

bank.q: Evaluate electrostatic, piezoelectric and shape-memory micro actuators for a MEMS RF switch; include pull-in, hysteresis, force and speed.
outline: Electrostatic: fast, low force, pull-in instability
Piezoelectric: fast, higher force, small strain
SMA: large motion, slow, hysteresis and heat
RF switch needs low loss, repeatability and reasonable voltage
answer: What the switch needs. A MEMS RF switch moves a beam or membrane about 1 to 3 µm to close or open a contact or capacitance. It must switch in microseconds, last billions of cycles, use almost no holding power, and be made by the same process as the rest of the chip.

answer.text: Electrostatic actuation. The plate force is F = ε₀AV²/(2g²). For a 200 µm × 200 µm plate, a 2 µm gap and 30 V:
Pull-in. The spring force kx rises linearly while the electric force rises as 1/g², so past a travel of g₀/3 the plate snaps down. For a spring constant k = 10 N/m:
answer.pre:
V<sub>PI</sub> = √(8 k g₀³ / (27 ε₀ A)) = √(8 × 10 × (2 × 10⁻⁶)³ / (27 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 4 × 10⁻⁸)) = 8.18 V
snap-down after 0.667 µm of travel; remaining gap 1.33 µm

answer: For a switch, pull-in is useful: the beam snaps fully closed for a firm contact. Holding needs only a voltage, so the power is almost zero (only leakage current), and release occurs at a lower voltage than pull-in, a small hysteresis that gives clean two-state action. Weaknesses: tens of volts are often needed (a charge pump on the chip), and charge trapped in the dielectric can make the beam stick.

Piezoelectric actuation. A PZT or AlN film strains when a field is applied. A stack of 100 layers, each moving 50 nm, gives 5.0 µm; a thin-film cantilever bends to a few micrometres at 3 to 10 V. Force is high and response is in microseconds, with no pull-in instability, so position is continuous. Weaknesses: PZT is hard to deposit in a standard process and contaminates CMOS, and ferroelectric hysteresis of 10 to 15 % and creep make the stroke depend on history.

Shape-memory actuation. A nitinol film or wire contracts 4 to 8 % when heated above its transformation temperature. It gives the largest force and stroke per volume, at low voltage. Weaknesses: it must be heated, so it uses milliwatts to watts; it cools slowly, so a cycle takes milliseconds to seconds; its thermal hysteresis is 10 to 30 °C; and it fatigues after about 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Criterion
Electrostatic
Piezoelectric
Shape memory
rows: ms to s, limited by cooling

answer: Recommendation. Electrostatic actuation for the RF switch. It switches in microseconds, holds at nearly zero power, is made by standard micromachining, and lasts billions of cycles; its pull-in instability is turned into an advantage, a positive snap to the closed state. Piezoelectric is the second choice where a low drive voltage matters more than process cost. Shape memory is rejected: it is too slow, needs continuous heating to hold, and fatigues within the switch's life.

Design notes. Keep the drive above VPI with margin (for example 12 V for an 8.18 V pull-in), reduce the hold voltage after closing to limit dielectric charging, and use a stiffer spring if a faster release is needed, since VPI rises as √k.
Check. Doubling k to 20 N/m raises VPI by √2 to 11.6 V; halving the gap to 1 µm lowers it by 2√2 to 2.89 V, because VPI goes as g₀3/2.

bank.q: Explain how a DSO captures a single fast pulse; compare with a CRO using bandwidth, sampling rate, memory and triggering.
outline: DSO samples and stores before display
Sampling rate must exceed signal bandwidth
Trigger and memory capture one-time events
CRO shows live trace but cannot store easily

answer.text: DSO block chain.
answer.pre:
probe → attenuator and amplifier (sets bandwidth) → ADC (sample rate) → acquisition memory (record length)
          ↑ trigger circuit decides which samples are kept → processor → LCD display, measurements, USB

answer: Capturing a single pulse. (a) Set single-shot (single sequence) mode. (b) Set the trigger to edge, on the expected slope and at a level halfway up the pulse. (c) The ADC runs continuously and writes into a circular memory. (d) When the trigger condition occurs, the scope keeps a set number of samples after it, then stops, so the record holds both pre-trigger samples (what happened before) and the pulse itself. (e) The stored trace stays on screen to be measured, zoomed and saved. An analogue CRO cannot do this: its spot draws the pulse once and the phosphor fades in milliseconds.

answer.text: Bandwidth and rise time. A scope with bandwidth BW has its own rise time tr ≈ 0.35/BW. The measured rise time is the root sum of squares:
answer.pre:
100 MHz scope: t<sub>r,scope</sub> = 0.35 / (100 × 10⁶) = 3.5 ns
pulse edge 5 ns: t<sub>measured</sub> = √(5² + 3.5²) = 6.10 ns, 22 % slow

answer: The rule is to use a bandwidth about five times the highest signal frequency, or a scope rise time a third to a fifth of the edge to be measured. The same 0.35/BW rule holds for a CRO; its vertical amplifier sets the bandwidth.

Sampling rate. A DSO needs several samples on the fastest edge: about 2.5 to 5 samples per period of the bandwidth for a repetitive signal, and more for a single shot because there is no second pass to fill the gaps. At 1 GS/s the samples are 1 ns apart, so a 5 ns edge gets five points. A CRO has no sampling: the trace is continuous.

answer.text: Memory. Record length = sample rate × time window. Too little memory forces the scope to slow its sampling when the time base is long.
answer.pre:
1 GS/s × 10 µs = 10 000 samples
with a 10 000-point memory, a 1 ms window drops the rate to 10 MS/s (100 ns per sample)

answer: Triggering. A CRO trigger only starts the sweep, and a non-repeating event shows once and is gone. A DSO trigger selects which part of the stored record to keep and can look before the event (pre-trigger). Advanced triggers (pulse width, runt, glitch, pattern) catch faults that an edge trigger misses.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Feature
Analogue CRO
DSO
rows: set by vertical amplifier and CRT, up to about 100 MHz
set by front end, 50 MHz to tens of GHz
automatic: rise time, frequency, RMS, FFT
aliasing if under-sampled; dead time between captures

answer: Medical note. A patient monitor is a slow DSO: it samples the ECG at a few hundred samples per second, stores it, and freezes a trace when an arrhythmia triggers the alarm.

Check. For a 5 ns edge measured within about 5 %, the scope rise time must be under a third of it, 1.67 ns, so BW ≥ 0.35 / 1.67 ns = 210 MHz; a 200 MHz scope gives √(5² + 1.75²) = 5.30 ns, 6 % slow, and a 350 MHz scope gives 5.10 ns, 2 % slow.

bank.q: A Kelvin bridge and a Wheatstone bridge are offered for 0.001 Ω measurement. Evaluate lead resistance, sensitivity and practical use.
outline: Wheatstone lead resistance adds error at low R
Kelvin bridge uses four-terminal connection
Kelvin separates current and voltage leads
Choose Kelvin for low resistance, Wheatstone for ordinary R

answer.text: Wheatstone bridge on 0.001 Ω. The bridge balances at Rx = R₃(R₂/R₁), but whatever lies in the Rx arm is measured. Two leads of 0.01 Ω each add 0.02 Ω:

answer: Contact resistance at the clamps (also milliohms) and thermal EMFs at the joints add more. The Wheatstone bridge is therefore used from about 1 Ω upward, where 0.02 Ω is 2 % or less.

Sensitivity of the Wheatstone bridge here. To keep the unknown from overheating, the current is limited, so the detector sees a tiny unbalance voltage. A 1 mΩ resistor at 10 A gives only 10 mV across itself, and a 0.1 % unbalance gives 10 µV at the detector, near the noise of an ordinary galvanometer.

Kelvin double bridge. The unknown Rx and a standard Rs of similar size are joined by a heavy link of resistance r and carry the same large current. Each has separate current and potential terminals (four-terminal connection). A second set of ratio arms a and b is connected to the potential terminals, so the voltage is sensed inside the current contacts.

answer.text: Balance condition.
answer.pre:
R<sub>x</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> (R₁/R₂) + [b r / (a + b + r)] (R₁/R₂ − a/b)
with a/b = R₁/R₂ the link term vanishes:  R<sub>x</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> R₁/R₂

answer.text: Worked balance. Standard Rs = 0.01 Ω, ratio arms R₁ = 100 Ω, R₂ = 1000 Ω, a = 100 Ω, b = 1000 Ω, test current 10 A:

answer: The lead resistance of the ratio arms (hundreds of ohms) is negligible, and the current-lead resistance carries current but is outside the measuring loop, so it causes no error.

Sensitivity of the Kelvin bridge. Because the error terms are gone, a large current (10 to 100 A) can be used, giving millivolts across Rx; a sensitive galvanometer or a nanovoltmeter detects the unbalance. Reversing the current and averaging cancels thermal EMFs.

answer.text: Evaluation.

head: Criterion
Wheatstone
Kelvin double bridge
rows: Lead and contact error at 1 mΩ
ammeter shunts, busbars, motor windings, cable joints, earth links

answer: Recommendation. The Kelvin bridge, or its modern form the four-terminal digital micro-ohmmeter. The Wheatstone bridge is rejected because its leads alone are twenty times the quantity to be measured.

Medical note. The same four-terminal (Kelvin) idea is used in bioimpedance measurement: two electrodes drive the current and two others sense the voltage, so skin contact resistance does not enter the reading.

Check. With the ratio arms mismatched by 1 % (a/b = 0.101) and a link of r = 0.001 Ω, the link term is (1000 × 0.001 / 1100.001)(0.1 − 0.101) = −0.91 µΩ, about 0.09 % of 1 mΩ, which is why the double bridge tolerates practical link resistance.

glossary.def: The processing of a sensor signal to make it suitable for transmission or digitisation.
A device that changes a physical quantity into an electrical output.
Analogue-to-digital converter; it turns a continuous voltage into a digital code.
The smallest input change an ADC or display can show, often one least significant bit.
The number of samples taken per second, measured in samples per second or hertz.
A low-pass filter placed before an ADC to remove frequencies above half the sampling rate.
Correction that makes a non-linear sensor output proportional to the measured quantity.
Separation that lets signal pass but blocks direct current paths between circuits.
Components that divert or clamp high-voltage transients before they damage a circuit.
Supervisory control and data acquisition; a distributed system for monitoring and controlling plant.
A current transmission standard with 4 mA at zero and 20 mA at full scale.
Two insulated wires twisted together so picked-up noise tends to cancel.
A tube and piston that produce linear force from compressed air.
A valve that sets the direction, pressure or flow of oil in a hydraulic circuit.
A valve opened or closed by a solenoid coil.
The moving and fixed metal pieces that open or close a relay circuit.
Voltage induced by a changing magnetic field when a coil current is switched off.
The fixed angle a stepper motor turns for one pulse, equal to 360° divided by steps per revolution.
A sensor signal that reports actual position or speed so the controller can correct error.
The voltage at which electrostatic force overcomes spring force and a micro plate snaps down.
A four-arm resistance bridge used to find an unknown resistance by null balance.
A four-terminal bridge that measures very low resistance without lead resistance error.
An AC bridge used to measure capacitance and loss angle of a capacitor.
Digital storage oscilloscope; it samples and stores waveforms for display and analysis.
An AC bridge for coils of high Q (above 10), with a series resistor and capacitor in the arm opposite the coil.
An AC bridge that compares an inductance with a capacitance in parallel with a resistor; best for Q from 1 to 10.
Common-mode rejection ratio: how strongly a differential amplifier rejects a voltage common to both inputs, 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub>) dB.
A band-stop filter with a narrow stop band, used to remove 50 Hz mains hum from an ECG.
An amplifier with no conducting path between input and output; rated by a test voltage and a lower continuous working voltage.
The number of samples a DSO stores per capture: sample rate times time window.
The spot movement on a CRT screen per volt on the deflecting plates, in mm/V.
